plain: A team of doctors and hospitals that shares in the savings if it keeps a group of patients healthy for less.
snappy: A provider group held jointly accountable for the cost and quality of a defined patient population, sharing in savings.
detail: An accountable care organization is a network of providers that agrees to manage a population's care and split the savings with the payer if it beats a cost target while hitting quality marks — and sometimes shares the losses if it doesn't. Medicare pioneered the model to push value-based care. It nudges hospitals and doctors to coordinate rather than each bill in isolation, the opposite of fee-for-service.

plain: What damaged property was worth at the moment it was lost — its replacement cost minus wear and tear.
snappy: A settlement basis equal to replacement cost minus depreciation, paying what the property was actually worth when lost.
detail: Total your ten-year-old roof and an actual cash value policy pays for a ten-year-old roof, not a new one — replacement cost less depreciation. It's cheaper to buy but leaves a gap you cover out of pocket. Many homeowners later wish they'd paid more for replacement cost coverage, especially on roofs, where insurers increasingly impose actual cash value to limit their payouts.

plain: The share of medical costs a health plan covers on average — the math behind the metal tiers.
snappy: The percentage of total covered costs a plan pays on average for a standard population, fixing its metal tier.
detail: A plan with 70% actuarial value — a silver plan — pays roughly 70% of a typical population's covered costs, leaving 30% to deductibles, copays, and coinsurance. It's an average across many people, not a promise for any one person. Actuaries compute it to slot plans into metal tiers so buyers can compare generosity at a glance. It's where insurance pricing meets the ACA's consumer-protection rules.

plain: Someone added to your policy so they're protected too — often a landlord or business partner who demands it.
snappy: A party other than the named insured granted coverage under the policy, usually by endorsement to satisfy a contract.
detail: Landlords, lenders, and clients routinely require that they be named on a tenant's or contractor's liability policy, so that it responds if they're sued over the work. The status is added by endorsement and usually doesn't raise the limit — the added party shares the coverage of the named insured. Construction contracts live and die on whether this language was drafted correctly.

plain: The 2010 health law that created online marketplaces, subsidies, and rules banning denial for pre-existing conditions.
snappy: The 2010 law overhauling US health coverage with marketplaces, premium subsidies, and guaranteed-issue protections.
detail: The Affordable Care Act reshaped individual health insurance: it set up the marketplaces where people buy subsidised plans, barred insurers from rejecting or surcharging pre-existing conditions, required plans to cover essential health benefits with no lifetime limits, and capped the out-of-pocket maximum. Premium tax credits make coverage affordable for many. It remains the backbone of how the uninsured and self-employed get covered, and a perennial political fight.

plain: The total an insurer will pay over the whole policy term, across all claims combined.
snappy: The maximum a policy pays for all covered losses during its term, separate from the per-occurrence limit on each event.
detail: A general liability policy might carry a $1 million per-occurrence limit and a $2 million aggregate: any one claim is capped at a million, and once total payouts reach two million the policy is exhausted for the year. A string of claims can burn through the aggregate and leave you bare before renewal. Knowing how much aggregate is left is vital when a second loss follows a first.

plain: The price your plan has decided a service is worth — the basis for what it and you actually pay.
snappy: The maximum a plan recognises as payable for a covered service; the negotiated rate on which cost-sharing is figured.
detail: The doctor may charge $300, but if your plan's allowed amount is $180, that's the number that matters: the plan pays its share of $180 and your coinsurance is figured on it. In-network providers write off the rest; out-of-network ones can bill you for it. The allowed amount appears on every explanation of benefits as the line between billed and covered.

plain: Your formal request asking the plan to reconsider after it denies a claim or service.
snappy: A challenge by the policyholder to a coverage denial, first reviewed internally and then, if needed, by an outside reviewer.
detail: When a plan denies a claim or refuses to authorise care, you have the right to appeal — first an internal review by the plan, then an external review by an independent third party whose decision the ACA makes binding. Many denials are overturned on appeal, yet most patients never file. Knowing the deadlines and attaching the doctor's supporting letter is how a wrongly denied claim gets paid.

plain: The form where you tell the insurer about yourself so it can decide whether and how to cover you.
snappy: The form on which a prospective insured discloses the facts underwriters use to accept, price, or decline the risk.
detail: The application is the foundation of utmost good faith: answer honestly, because a material misrepresentation here can let the insurer rescind the policy and refuse a claim later. Underwriters lean on it to classify the risk and set the premium. For life and disability cover the application may trigger a medical exam and a check of prescription and claims databases before an offer is made.

plain: When an insurer treats you unfairly — denying or dragging out a valid claim — and can be punished for it.
snappy: Unreasonable handling of a claim or defence by an insurer, exposing it to damages beyond the policy limit.
detail: Insurers owe their policyholders good faith and fair dealing. Deny a clearly covered claim, lowball a settlement, or refuse to defend without grounds and the insured can sue for bad faith, recovering not just the claim but extra-contractual and sometimes punitive damages. The threat keeps carriers honest and is why a reasonable but wrong denial is defensible while an arbitrary one is dangerous.

plain: When an out-of-network provider bills you for the gap between their charge and what your plan paid.
snappy: Charging a patient the difference between a provider's full charge and the plan's allowed amount, common out-of-network.
detail: Balance billing hits when an out-of-network provider charges $1,000, the plan's allowed amount is $400, and you're billed the $600 gap on top of your cost-share. It produced the notorious surprise bills from out-of-network emergency-room doctors at in-network hospitals. The No Surprises Act now bars it in many of those situations, but it still applies when you knowingly choose an out-of-network provider.

plain: The person who collects the money when a life insurance policy pays out.
snappy: The person or entity designated to receive the proceeds of a life insurance policy or annuity when the insured dies.
detail: You name a beneficiary when you buy life insurance — a spouse, child, trust, or charity. Primary beneficiaries get paid first; contingent ones inherit only if the primary has died. Keeping the designation current is critical: proceeds go to whoever is named on the form, not whoever a will lists, which is why divorces and remarriages trigger so many disputed payouts. The named beneficiary generally takes the money free of income tax.

plain: Temporary proof you're covered right now, before the full policy paperwork arrives.
snappy: A short-term agreement providing immediate coverage while the formal policy is being written and issued.
detail: When you buy a car at noon, the agent issues a binder so you can legally drive it home before the printed policy exists. A binder carries the same coverage as the policy it stands in for, but only for a set period — often 30 to 90 days — until the real document is issued or declined. Lenders accept a binder as proof of insurance at a closing.

plain: A workplace benefits menu that lets you pay for health coverage and other perks with pre-tax dollars.
snappy: An employer benefit plan under tax code Section 125 letting employees choose benefits and pay with pre-tax salary.
detail: A cafeteria plan, named for its pick-and-choose menu, lets workers fund health premiums, a flexible spending account, or dependent care with pre-tax salary, cutting their taxable income. It's the tax plumbing behind most employer benefit enrollments. The Section 125 rules govern what can be offered and when elections can change — which is why mid-year benefit changes usually require a qualifying life event.

plain: Ending a policy before its term is up — by you or the insurer.
snappy: Termination of a policy before its expiration date, by the insured or, for limited reasons, by the insurer.
detail: You can usually cancel anytime and get back the unused premium. An insurer's power to cancel mid-term is tightly limited by state law — typically only for non-payment, fraud, or a big rise in the risk — because pulling coverage out from under someone is drastic. After a short initial window, most policies can't be cancelled for ordinary claims; the insurer must wait and nonrenew instead.

plain: Paying a doctor a fixed monthly amount per patient instead of per service.
snappy: A payment model paying providers a set amount per enrolled patient per period, regardless of services actually used.
detail: Under capitation, a plan pays a primary care physician a flat monthly fee for each assigned patient, whether that patient is seen ten times or never. It flips the incentive of fee-for-service: the provider profits by keeping patients healthy and avoiding unnecessary care, but bears the risk if they get sick. Common in HMOs and accountable care arrangements, it's central to the shift toward value-based care.

plain: A bare-bones, low-premium health plan for young or low-income people that mainly guards against disaster.
snappy: A low-premium, high-deductible ACA plan, limited to those under 30 or with a hardship exemption, covering worst-case costs.
detail: A catastrophic plan carries the lowest premium and a deductible near the out-of-pocket maximum, so it pays little until a serious illness or accident. It still covers essential health benefits and a few preventive visits and primary-care visits. Only people under 30 or those with a hardship exemption can buy one, and premium tax credits don't apply, which limits its appeal to the young and healthy.

plain: Low-cost government health coverage for kids in families that earn too much for Medicaid but can't easily afford private plans.
snappy: A federal-state program covering children in families above Medicaid limits but below private-coverage affordability.
detail: CHIP fills the gap just above Medicaid eligibility, covering checkups, immunisations, dental, and hospital care for children at low or no cost. States run it alongside Medicaid, sometimes as an extension of it. It enjoys rare bipartisan support and covers millions of kids whose parents earn modestly. Families often discover it when they apply for Medicaid and the children qualify even if the adults don't.

plain: A formal request asking your insurer to pay for a loss the policy covers.
snappy: A demand by the insured (or a third party) for payment under the policy after a covered loss occurs.
detail: Filing a claim starts the payout process: you report the loss, an adjuster investigates, and the insurer pays, partly pays, or denies. Filing too many makes your premium rise or renewal harder. The word also means the eventual cost an insurer bears: "claims came in higher than expected this quarter" is the line that sinks an insurance stock when catastrophes strike.

plain: Whoever is asking the insurer to pay — you, or the person you injured.
snappy: The party making a claim for payment, whether the policyholder (first-party) or an injured outsider (third-party).
detail: In a first-party claim the claimant is the insured asking their own carrier to pay, as when you report a stolen laptop. In a third-party claim the claimant is the outsider you harmed — the driver you rear-ended files against your liability coverage. Adjusters separate the two because their duties differ: they owe good faith to their own insured, and only fair dealing to a third-party claimant.

plain: Liability cover that only pays if the claim is reported while the policy is active.
snappy: A liability policy that responds only to claims first made and reported during its term, often with a retroactive date.
detail: Doctors and professionals usually carry claims-made coverage: it's cheaper at first but the trigger is when the claim is filed, not when the mistake happened. Let the policy end and an old error becomes uninsured unless you buy tail coverage. A retroactive date sets how far back covered acts can reach. Switching carriers requires careful handling so no period falls through the gap.

plain: A law letting you keep your job's health plan for a while after you leave — but you pay the full premium.
snappy: A federal law letting workers and families continue group coverage after job loss, at their own full cost plus a fee.
detail: Lose or leave a job and COBRA lets you keep the same group health plan, usually for up to 18 months — but now you pay the entire premium the employer used to subsidise, plus a 2% fee, so the sticker shock is real. It bridges the gap until new coverage or a special enrollment period. Many people compare the COBRA cost with a marketplace plan and find the subsidised marketplace cheaper.

plain: The share of a covered bill you keep paying even after the deductible — often a percentage.
snappy: A cost-sharing percentage the insured pays after the deductible; in property, a clause penalising under-insurance.
detail: In health insurance, 20% coinsurance means after your deductible you pay a fifth of each bill until you hit the out-of-pocket maximum. In property insurance the word means something different: a coinsurance clause requires you to insure a building to a set percentage of its value (often 80%) or the insurer pays only part of even a small loss. Same word, two traps for the unwary.

plain: Pricing that charges everyone in an area the same, instead of charging sick people more.
snappy: Setting premiums by geography and a few allowed factors rather than individual health, so the sick aren't priced out.
detail: Under the ACA's modified community rating, insurers can vary individual premiums only by area, age, family size, and tobacco use — not by health or gender. It spreads the cost of the sick across the whole pool, the flip side of guaranteed issue. Pure community rating would charge literally everyone the same; the modified version keeps age bands. It's why a 20-year-old and a 60-year-old pay different but capped-ratio premiums.

plain: The fine-print duties you must meet — like reporting a loss promptly — or the insurer can refuse to pay.
snappy: Policy provisions setting out the duties and procedures the insured must follow for coverage to apply.
detail: Notify the insurer promptly, cooperate with the investigation, protect property from further damage, submit a proof of loss on time — these strings are attached to every grant of coverage. Break a material one and the insurer may deny an otherwise valid claim. This section is also where you find how disputes are resolved, how other insurance is coordinated, and the right of the insurer to inspect or audit.

plain: The rules that decide which plan pays first when you're covered by two of them.
snappy: Rules determining the order in which two or more health plans pay when a person is covered by more than one.
detail: When a child is on both parents' plans, or a worker has employer coverage plus a spouse's, coordination of benefits sets which plan is primary and pays first and which is secondary and picks up the remainder. The goal is to stop double payment while making sure the patient isn't shortchanged. The "birthday rule" — the parent whose birthday falls earlier in the year pays first — is the classic tiebreaker for kids.

plain: A flat fee — say $25 — you hand over at the doctor or pharmacy, with insurance covering the rest.
snappy: A fixed dollar amount the insured pays for a covered health service, separate from the deductible and coinsurance.
detail: A $30 copay for a primary-care visit or $10 for a generic drug is predictable, which is why plans use copays for routine care — you know the cost before you walk in. Copays may or may not count toward your deductible, but they do count toward the out-of-pocket maximum. You'll see them printed on your insurance card next to the network type so the front desk knows what to collect.

plain: Extra help on a marketplace plan that shrinks your deductible and copays if your income is low enough.
snappy: An ACA subsidy that lowers deductibles, copays, and the out-of-pocket maximum for lower-income silver-plan enrollees.
detail: On top of the premium tax credit, a cost-sharing reduction quietly upgrades a silver marketplace plan for lower-income buyers — slashing the deductible, copays, and out-of-pocket maximum so the plan pays a bigger share of each bill. You must pick a silver plan to get it. Many eligible people miss out by choosing bronze for the lower premium, not realising they're leaving this help on the table.

plain: The protection your policy actually provides — the specific losses it promises to pay for.
snappy: The scope of protection a policy grants: which perils, people, and property it pays for, up to stated limits.
detail: Coverage is what you're buying. A homeowners policy might pay for fire and theft but not flood; an auto policy splits protection into liability, collision, and comprehensive. Agents talk about "gaps in coverage" when a real-world loss falls outside every section of the policy. Reading which coverages you have — and at what limit — is the difference between a paid claim and an unpleasant surprise.

plain: A policy that pays a lump sum of cash if you're diagnosed with a serious illness like cancer or a heart attack.
snappy: Supplemental coverage paying a fixed cash benefit on diagnosis of a covered serious illness, used however the insured wishes.
detail: Critical illness insurance pays a tax-free lump sum — say $20,000 — on diagnosis of a covered condition such as cancer, heart attack, or stroke, no matter your medical bills. The cash can cover the deductible, lost income, or travel for treatment. Sold as a cheap voluntary benefit at work, it plugs gaps a high-deductible health plan leaves. Critics note the narrow list of covered conditions and the fine print on what counts.

plain: The front page of your policy listing who's covered, for what, and for how much.
snappy: The summary page of the policy stating the named insured, coverages, limits, deductibles, premium, and policy period.
detail: The declarations page — "the dec page" — is the cheat sheet agents pull up first. It personalises the standard policy form with your name, address, vehicle or building, the coverages you bought, their limits and deductibles, and the premium. A lender asking for "proof of insurance" usually wants this page. If a fact here is wrong, the policy may not respond the way you expect when you file a claim.

plain: The slice of a loss you pay yourself before the insurer pays the rest.
snappy: A fixed amount the insured absorbs on each claim before coverage kicks in; higher deductibles mean lower premiums.
detail: If your car repair costs $3,000 and your deductible is $500, you pay $500 and the insurer pays $2,500. It keeps small nuisance claims off the books and gives you a reason to drive carefully. Choosing a higher figure lowers your premium because you're shouldering more of the risk. Health, auto, and homeowners policies all use this tool, though health plans layer on coinsurance and copays too.

plain: A plan that helps pay for cleanings, fillings, and bigger dental work, usually with a low annual cap.
snappy: Coverage for dental care, typically with full preventive cleanings but a low annual maximum on major work.
detail: Dental insurance works differently from medical: it usually covers preventive cleanings fully, basic work like fillings at a share, and major work like crowns at half — all under a low annual maximum, often around $1,500. Hit the cap and you pay the rest yourself. It's commonly sold as a standalone or employer add-on, and the modest limits mean it cushions routine care more than it protects against catastrophe.

plain: The drop in an item's value as it ages and wears — subtracted when a policy pays actual cash value.
snappy: The decline in property value from age, wear, and obsolescence, deducted from replacement cost to reach actual cash value.
detail: A claims adjuster paying actual cash value depreciates your loss: a sofa half through its useful life is paid at roughly half its new price. The recoverable portion is what a replacement-cost policy holds back and releases once you rebuild. Arguments over how fast a roof or appliance wears are among the most common sticking points in property claims.

plain: Income protection that pays you part of your paycheck if illness or injury keeps you from working.
snappy: Coverage replacing a portion of earned income when illness or injury prevents the insured from working.
detail: Disability insurance protects the asset most people forget — their ability to earn. Short-term policies cover weeks to months; long-term ones can pay to retirement age, typically replacing 50–70% of income after an elimination period. Employers often provide a base layer, which workers supplement individually. It matters most for those whose savings couldn't survive a year off work, and the definition of "disabled" in the policy decides whether a claim pays.

plain: The promise by your insurer to hire and pay lawyers to fight a covered lawsuit against you.
snappy: An obligation on a liability insurer to provide and fund a legal defence for claims that potentially fall within coverage.
detail: The duty to defend is broader than the duty to pay: an insurer must defend a lawsuit if any allegation might be covered, even if it later proves it owes nothing. Defence costs often dwarf the eventual settlement, so this promise is a big part of a liability policy's value. Refuse to defend wrongly and the insurer risks a bad-faith judgment far above the policy limit.

plain: The slice of premium an insurer has truly earned because that part of the coverage period has already passed.
snappy: The portion of a prepaid premium an insurer has earned as time elapses, recognised as revenue over the policy period.
detail: Pay $1,200 for a year of cover and after one month the insurer has earned $100; the other $1,100 is unearned premium it would refund if you cancelled. Insurers report earned premium as revenue and measure their loss ratio against it. The distinction matters at cancellation and in accounting, where booking premium before it's earned overstates how well a carrier is really doing.

plain: The day your coverage switches on.
snappy: The calendar date coverage under a policy begins; losses before it are not covered even if the premium is paid.
detail: Coverage doesn't exist until the effective date, which is why buyers time it to the moment they take the car keys or close on a house. Backdating is generally barred to stop people insuring a loss that already happened. Lenders and motor-vehicle offices check it against the purchase to be sure there was never an uninsured gap.

plain: The waiting stretch after you become disabled before benefit payments start.
snappy: The time between a disability or claim trigger and the start of benefit payments, functioning like a time-based deductible.
detail: On a disability policy, the elimination period is how long you must be unable to work before benefits begin — often 90 days, sometimes longer for long-term coverage. A longer elimination period lowers the premium, the same trade-off as a higher deductible. It exists to keep small, short claims off the insurer and to make you self-insure the first stretch. Long-term care policies use the same waiting-period mechanism.

plain: An add-on that changes your policy — adding, removing, or tweaking what's covered.
snappy: A written amendment to a policy that adds, restricts, or modifies coverage; also called a rider in life and health.
detail: Add a home office, schedule a wedding ring, or buy back flood coverage and the insurer issues an endorsement that becomes part of the contract. It can expand coverage or quietly cut it, so reading the change at renewal matters. Standardised industry forms mean the same numbered amendment carries identical wording across many carriers, which is why agents quote them by code.

plain: A middle-ground health plan: no referrals needed, but it only pays for its own network of doctors.
snappy: A plan that, like a PPO, needs no referrals but, like an HMO, covers only in-network care outside emergencies.
detail: An EPO splits the difference between HMO and PPO. You don't need a primary care physician or referrals to see specialists, but step outside the network for anything but an emergency and you pay the full bill. Premiums sit between an HMO and a PPO. It suits people who want freedom from referrals but can live within a defined network to keep costs down.

plain: The 1974 federal law that governs most employer-sponsored health and retirement benefits.
snappy: The federal law setting standards for private-sector benefit plans and pre-empting state regulation of self-funded plans.
detail: ERISA sets the ground rules for employer health and pension plans — disclosure, fiduciary duty, and an appeals process for denied claims. Crucially, it pre-empts state insurance law for self-funded plans, which is why a big employer's coverage can skip state mandates. When a denied claim heads to federal court rather than a state insurance commissioner, ERISA is the reason. It shapes the legal backdrop of nearly all job-based benefits.

plain: The ten categories of care every marketplace plan must cover — from hospital stays to maternity to mental health.
snappy: Ten benefit categories the ACA requires individual and small-group plans to cover, from emergency care to prescriptions.
detail: Before the ACA, plans could skip maternity care or prescription drugs to cut premiums. Essential health benefits force every individual and small-group plan to cover ten categories — hospitalisation, emergency care, maternity, mental health, prescriptions, preventive care, and more — with no annual or lifetime dollar limits. The rule is why a cheap plan can't simply carve out the expensive things you might actually need.

plain: Coverage that only pays after an underlying policy limit is used up.
snappy: A policy that responds above a stated attachment point, paying only once the underlying coverage is exhausted.
detail: A factory needing $50 million of liability cover stacks layers: a primary policy to $5 million, then excess policies for each band above. Each excess insurer pays only when the layer beneath is spent, so its premium is lower per dollar of limit. Towers of excess insurance are how big risks get covered when no single carrier wants the whole exposure.

plain: A loss your policy specifically refuses to cover, listed in black and white.
snappy: A clause carving a peril, property, or circumstance out of coverage; the first place an adjuster looks to deny a claim.
detail: Every policy has exclusions — flood and earthquake on a standard homeowners policy, intentional acts, war, normal wear and tear. They exist to keep premiums affordable and to push uninsurable or specialist risks into separate policies. When a claim is denied, the denial letter cites the exclusion by number. Knowing yours is how you discover you need a flood policy or a separate rider before the loss, not after.

plain: The day your coverage runs out unless you renew.
snappy: The date coverage under a policy ends; without renewal or extension, the insured is bare from that moment on.
detail: Miss the expiration date without renewing and you're uninsured the next morning, even if you never meant to cancel. Carriers send renewal offers weeks ahead; ignoring them is the most common way people accidentally let coverage drop. Claims-made liability policies make the date doubly important because reporting a claim after expiration — without tail coverage — leaves old work unprotected.

plain: The statement your plan sends after a claim showing what was billed, what it paid, and what you owe.
snappy: A post-claim statement detailing the billed charge, allowed amount, plan payment, and the patient's remaining responsibility.
detail: An explanation of benefits is not a bill — it's the plan's accounting of a processed claim: the provider's charge, the allowed amount, what the plan paid, and what counts toward your deductible and out-of-pocket maximum. Reading it catches errors and surprise charges before the provider's actual bill arrives. The words "not a bill" are printed at the top precisely because so many people mistake it for one.

plain: How much potential loss an insurer is on the hook for — the size of the bet it took.
snappy: The measure of potential loss an insurer carries, by policy, peril, or region; the base on which premium is calculated.
detail: An insurer measures hurricane exposure as the total it could pay if one storm hit every coastal home it covers. The word also names the rating base — payroll for workers' comp, sales for product liability, square footage for a building — that scales the premium. Managing accumulated exposure in one zip code or one peril is why carriers buy reinsurance and cap how much they'll write in a single area.

plain: An independent outside opinion you can demand when your plan upholds a denial.
snappy: An independent third-party review of a denied claim after internal appeals fail, with a decision binding on the plan.
detail: If the plan denies your internal appeal, external review hands the dispute to an independent organisation with no stake in the outcome, and the ACA makes its decision binding. It's the backstop against an insurer marking its own homework. Patients use it most for denials of expensive or experimental treatments. The plan must tell you how to request it on every final denial notice.

plain: Paying doctors for each individual test, visit, or procedure they perform.
snappy: The traditional model paying providers per service rendered, rewarding volume rather than outcomes.
detail: Fee-for-service is the default that pays a provider for every visit, scan, and procedure — simple, but it rewards doing more rather than doing what helps. Critics blame it for driving up US health spending, which is why payers push value-based care and capitation as alternatives. Original Medicare still runs largely on fee-for-service, the benchmark every payment reform is measured against.

plain: Insurance that pays you for your own losses.
snappy: Coverage that pays the insured directly for their own damage or loss, as opposed to liability owed to outsiders.
detail: Collision coverage that fixes your own car, the dwelling coverage that rebuilds your own house, the health plan that pays your own hospital bill — these are first-party. The insurer owes its own policyholder a duty of good faith in handling them. First-party claims contrast with third-party liability claims, where the policy pays someone else you harmed.

plain: A use-it-or-lose-it workplace account that lets you set aside pre-tax money for medical costs.
snappy: An employer account funding medical or dependent-care costs with pre-tax dollars, generally forfeited if unused by year-end.
detail: A flexible spending account lets employees route pre-tax salary toward out-of-pocket medical costs, lowering taxable income. The catch is the use-it-or-lose-it rule: unspent funds are largely forfeited at year-end, give or take a small carryover or grace period. Unlike a health savings account it needs no high-deductible plan but doesn't roll over freely. December brings the annual rush to spend down the balance on glasses and prescriptions.

plain: Your plan's list of covered medications, sorted into price tiers.
snappy: The list of prescription drugs a plan covers, organised into tiers that set each drug's copay or coinsurance.
detail: The formulary decides whether your medication is covered and how much you pay for it. Drugs sit in tiers — generics cheapest, preferred brands next, specialty drugs priciest — and a pharmacy benefit manager negotiates the list. A drug left off the formulary may need a prior authorization, a step-therapy trial, or an appeal. People with chronic conditions check the formulary before choosing a plan each open enrollment.

plain: The main doctor who must approve your access to specialists in a managed-care plan.
snappy: The primary care physician in a managed plan whose referral controls whether specialist care is covered.
detail: In a gatekeeper model — classic HMO design — your primary care physician is the hub: you can't get covered specialist care without going through them for a referral. It controls cost and coordinates care but frustrates patients who know exactly which specialist they need. PPOs drop the gatekeeper, letting members self-refer for a higher premium. The term captures the central cost-control bargain of managed care.

plain: Extra days after a missed payment when your coverage still counts.
snappy: A short window after the premium due date during which coverage continues and a late payment keeps the policy alive.
detail: Life insurance typically grants a 30- or 31-day grace period; if the insured dies during it, the insurer pays the benefit minus the owed premium. Health and other policies have their own grace windows, lengthened for subsidised marketplace plans. The grace period is the safety net between a missed payment and a full lapse — pay inside it and nothing is lost.

plain: Health coverage you get through an employer, where the risk is spread across all the workers.
snappy: Employer- or association-sponsored coverage where a pooled group shares risk, usually with the employer paying part of the premium.
detail: Most working-age adults get coverage through group health insurance at a job, where the employer negotiates with an insurer and pays a chunk of the premium pre-tax. Pooling many employees spreads risk and avoids individual medical underwriting. Lose the job and COBRA or a special enrollment period bridges the gap. The tax break for employer coverage is the quiet reason US health insurance is tied to employment.

plain: A rule that an insurer must sell you a policy regardless of your health.
snappy: A requirement that insurers offer coverage to any applicant, regardless of health status or pre-existing conditions.
detail: Guaranteed issue is the engine behind the pre-existing-condition protection: in the ACA individual market, insurers must accept all comers during open enrollment and can't screen out the sick. It only works paired with community rating and broad enrollment, or healthy people wait until they're ill to buy — the adverse-selection problem the individual mandate was meant to solve. Medicare supplement plans have their own narrower guaranteed-issue windows.

plain: A condition that makes a loss more likely or worse — a frayed wire, an icy step, a smoker's habit.
snappy: A condition that increases the chance or severity of a loss from a peril; underwriters grade physical, moral, and morale hazards.
detail: If fire is the peril, the stacked oily rags in the basement are the hazard. Underwriters sort the kinds: physical ones are tangible (bald tyres, old wiring), moral ones are dishonest motives (insuring a failing business hoping it burns), and morale ones are carelessness born of having coverage. Spotting them lets insurers price, exclude, or require fixes before they'll write the risk.

plain: A plan that pays a share of your medical bills in exchange for a monthly premium.
snappy: Coverage that pays for medical care — doctors, hospitals, drugs — in return for premiums and patient cost-sharing.
detail: Health insurance is the most-used and least-understood policy most people own. You pay a premium, then share costs through a deductible, copays, and coinsurance until you reach the out-of-pocket maximum. Which doctors are in-network, what the formulary covers, and whether a service needs prior authorization all decide your real bill. You'll wrestle with it every open enrollment and every time a claim is denied.

plain: The government website where individuals shop for plans and claim subsidies.
snappy: An ACA-created online exchange where individuals compare and buy health plans and apply for premium tax credits.
detail: The marketplace — healthcare.gov or a state-run exchange — is where the self-employed and uninsured browse standardised plans sorted into metal tiers and find out if they qualify for a premium tax credit. Plans are guaranteed issue, so a pre-existing condition can't keep you out. You can usually only enroll during open enrollment unless a qualifying life event opens a special enrollment period.

plain: The specific insurance product covering your medical care, with its own network, rules, and prices.
snappy: A specific health insurance product defining its network, covered benefits, cost-sharing, and premium.
detail: When HR says "pick a plan," each option is a health plan with a different premium, deductible, network, and formulary. Plans come in types — HMO, PPO, EPO, high-deductible — that trade lower premiums for tighter rules. Comparing the metal tier, the out-of-pocket maximum, and whether your doctors are in-network matters far more than the headline premium. The choice locks in for the year unless a qualifying life event opens a special enrollment period.

plain: An account your employer funds to reimburse you for medical costs or even your own insurance premiums.
snappy: An employer-funded, employer-owned arrangement reimbursing employees for qualified medical costs or individual premiums.
detail: Unlike a health savings account, a health reimbursement arrangement is funded and owned by the employer, which reimburses workers tax-free for medical expenses. Newer individual-coverage versions let small employers give workers money to buy their own marketplace plan instead of offering a group plan. It shifts plan choice to the employee while capping the employer's cost — a model spreading among small businesses.

plain: A tax-free savings account for medical costs, available only if you have a high-deductible health plan.
snappy: A tax-advantaged account for medical expenses, paired with a qualifying high-deductible plan, with funds that roll over.
detail: A health savings account is the rare triple tax break: contributions go in pre-tax, grow untaxed, and come out tax-free for medical costs. You must have a high-deductible health plan to open one, and unspent money rolls over year to year and is yours to keep, even into retirement. Savers treat it as a stealth retirement account; the cash-strapped use it to cushion the deductible.

plain: A plan with low premiums but a big deductible you must pay before most coverage starts — usually paired with a tax-free savings account.
snappy: A plan with a high deductible and lower premium, meeting IRS limits so it can be paired with a health savings account.
detail: A high-deductible health plan keeps the monthly premium low and asks you to cover more upfront before coverage kicks in beyond preventive care. Because it meets federal thresholds, it unlocks a health savings account where you stash tax-free dollars for medical costs. The bet suits the healthy and the saver; a bad year means paying the full deductible before the plan pays much. Employers increasingly default to them.

plain: A health plan that's cheaper but keeps you inside its own doctor network and routes care through one main doctor.
snappy: A managed-care plan with low cost-sharing that covers only in-network providers and routes care through a primary care physician.
detail: An HMO trades flexibility for price: you pick a primary care physician who coordinates your care and writes referrals to see specialists, and out-of-network care isn't covered except in emergencies. Premiums and copays run lower than a PPO, with little paperwork when you stay inside the network. You'll hear it weighed against a PPO every open enrollment — the classic cost-versus-freedom choice.

plain: A supplemental plan that pays you a set cash amount for each day you're hospitalised.
snappy: Supplemental coverage paying a fixed daily or per-event cash benefit for hospital stays, regardless of actual charges.
detail: Hospital indemnity insurance pays a flat sum — perhaps $200 a day — directly to you for each day admitted, on top of whatever your health plan pays. The cash offsets the deductible, copays, or the everyday bills that pile up during a stay. It's a popular voluntary add-on for people with high-deductible health plans, though the payouts are modest and it's no substitute for real medical coverage.

plain: Doctors and hospitals your plan has a contract with, where your costs are lowest.
snappy: Providers contracted with your plan at negotiated rates, where cost-sharing is lowest and balance billing is barred.
detail: Staying in-network is the single biggest lever on what you actually pay. In-network providers accept the plan's negotiated rate as full payment, so you owe only your deductible, copay, or coinsurance — never the gap. The plan publishes a directory, but it can be out of date, so confirm before each visit. Out-of-network care flips all of this and can leave you with a surprise bill.

plain: The core idea that insurance restores you to where you were before the loss — no better, no worse.
snappy: The principle that insurance compensates actual loss to make the insured whole, without allowing a profit from misfortune.
detail: Indemnity is why a claim pays the depreciated value of a five-year-old roof, not the cost of a brand-new house. It stops insurance becoming a betting slip: you can't collect more than you lost, and insurable interest plus the indemnity principle keep people from profiting on a loss. Life insurance is the great exception — a life has no market value, so those policies pay a fixed agreed sum instead.

plain: The requirement that you'd actually suffer if the insured thing were lost — you can't insure a stranger's car.
snappy: A stake in the insured person or property such that its loss would cause the policyholder genuine financial harm.
detail: Insurable interest stops insurance becoming gambling: you can insure your own house, your spouse's life, or your business partner, but not a celebrity you've never met. In property cover the interest must exist at the time of loss; in life insurance, at the time the policy is bought. Courts void policies sold without it, a rule that traces back centuries to stamp out wagering on strangers' deaths.

plain: A deal where many people pay small amounts into a shared pot so the unlucky few who suffer a big loss get paid from it.
snappy: A contract that trades a small, certain payment — the premium — for protection against a large, uncertain loss.
detail: Insurance pools money from many policyholders so the few who suffer fires, crashes, illnesses, or deaths are paid from the common fund. You pay a premium; in exchange the insurer promises to cover specified losses up to a policy limit. It is the financial backbone behind mortgages, car keys, hospital visits, and business deals — every lender, landlord, or regulator who demands proof of coverage is relying on this bargain.

plain: The person or business the policy protects — usually you.
snappy: The person or entity whose interests a policy protects and who is entitled to file claims under it.
detail: The insured is who the coverage is for. On a homeowners policy it's the homeowner; on a commercial policy it might be a company plus its officers. The named insured (the one listed on the declarations page) has the most rights and duties, while additional insureds get a narrower slice. When a policy says "the insured must cooperate," it means you must help the adjuster investigate the claim.

plain: The company that takes your premium and promises to pay your covered losses.
snappy: The company that accepts the risk, collects premiums, and pays claims; also called the carrier or underwriter.
detail: The insurer is the party on the hook. It pools your premium with thousands of others, invests the float, and pays out when covered losses hit. Regulators watch its solvency closely because a failed insurer leaves policyholders stranded. You'll hear it called the "carrier" in agent-speak, and a single large risk may be split among several carriers, each taking a layer.

plain: The core promise of the policy — the sentence where the insurer says what it will pay for.
snappy: The section of a policy stating the central promise of the insurer to pay for specified losses in exchange for premium.
detail: Everything else in the policy — exclusions, conditions, definitions — modifies this one promise. Broad insuring agreements ("we cover all risks of direct physical loss") start wide and then carve back through exclusions; narrow ones ("we cover these named perils") start small. Coverage lawyers read the insuring agreement first to see whether a loss even gets in the door before the exclusions are argued.

plain: Losing your coverage because you stopped paying the premium.
snappy: Termination of a policy for non-payment of premium, leaving the insured uncovered until reinstatement or rebuy.
detail: Miss a premium past the grace period and the policy lapses — coverage stops, and a loss the next day isn't paid. A lapsed life policy can sometimes be reinstated by catching up payments and proving you're still healthy, but a lapse in auto coverage flags you as high-risk and raises your next premium. Lenders monitor for lapses and may force-place expensive coverage if yours drops.

plain: Coverage for help with daily living — nursing homes, home aides — when age or illness leaves you unable to cope alone.
snappy: Insurance paying for custodial care (nursing home, assisted living, home aides) that health insurance and Medicare won't.
detail: Long-term care insurance fills a gap that blindsides families: regular health insurance and Medicare don't pay for the years of help bathing, dressing, or eating that ageing or chronic illness can require. Policies pay a daily benefit toward a nursing home, assisted living, or home aide after an elimination period. Premiums are steep and rise with age, and the industry has struggled with mispriced older policies, making it a fraught but important purchase.

plain: The damage, injury, or cost that triggers a claim.
snappy: The harm an insurance policy responds to — damage, injury, liability, or death — measured in dollars for settlement.
detail: Loss is the event insurance exists to soften: a kitchen fire, a fender-bender, a hospital stay, a lawsuit. Insurers track "incurred losses" — what claims will ultimately cost — against the premium they collected, the ratio that decides whether a line of business makes money. A "total loss" means the damage exceeds the property's value, so the insurer pays the value rather than repairing.

plain: Health coverage that controls cost and quality by steering you to certain doctors and approving care in advance.
snappy: Systems that contain cost and coordinate care through provider networks, utilisation review, and primary-care gatekeeping.
detail: Managed care is the umbrella over HMOs, PPOs, and EPOs — the idea that an insurer actively manages care rather than just paying bills. Its tools are networks, referrals, prior authorization, and utilisation review, all aimed at cutting unnecessary spending. Praised for restraining costs and blamed for hassle and denials, it has defined US health insurance since the 1990s. Nearly every modern plan is some flavour of it.

plain: A false answer big enough that, had the insurer known the truth, it would have charged more or said no.
snappy: An untrue statement on an application important enough to have changed the decision of the insurer to cover or price the risk.
detail: Forget to mention a speeding ticket and it may not matter; hide a heart condition on a life application and the insurer can rescind the policy and deny the death claim. The test is materiality — whether the truth would have changed the underwriting decision. Insurers must usually act within a contestability window, after which even a misstatement can no longer undo the policy.

plain: The joint federal-state program providing free or low-cost health coverage to low-income people.
snappy: A means-tested public program, funded by states and the federal government, covering low-income and disabled people.
detail: Medicaid covers tens of millions — low-income families, pregnant women, people with disabilities, and, in expansion states, most low-income adults. States run it within federal rules, so benefits and eligibility vary widely. It pays for most US nursing-home care, the reason middle-class families encounter it through elder care. The ACA's Medicaid expansion, which states can accept or refuse, drove much of the drop in the uninsured rate.

plain: The share of your premiums an insurer must spend on actual care, not overhead — or it owes you a rebate.
snappy: The portion of premium an insurer spends on medical care and quality; the ACA sets minimums of 80–85%.
detail: The ACA forces insurers to spend at least 80% of individual and small-group premiums (85% for large groups) on care and quality improvement rather than administration, marketing, and profit. Fall short and they must rebate the difference to policyholders — those late-summer cheques some people receive. The medical loss ratio caps how much of your premium can become overhead, a rare direct check on insurer margins.

plain: The standard a service must meet — genuinely needed to treat your condition — for the plan to cover it.
snappy: Care a plan deems appropriate and required to diagnose or treat a condition per accepted standards; the test for coverage.
detail: "Medically necessary" is the gate every claim must pass: the plan covers care that's needed and appropriate, not elective or experimental. Utilization review applies the standard, and disputes over it drive a huge share of denials and appeals. The definition lives in the policy, so a treatment your doctor recommends can still be refused if the plan's reviewer judges it unnecessary, which is exactly what the appeals process exists to contest.

plain: The federal health program covering people 65 and older, and some younger people with disabilities.
snappy: The US federal health insurance program for those 65+ and certain disabled people, organised into four parts.
detail: Medicare is the backbone of US coverage for seniors: Medicare Part A covers hospital stays, Medicare Part B covers doctors and outpatient care, Medicare Part C (Medicare Advantage) bundles them through a private plan, and Medicare Part D covers drugs. Original Medicare leaves gaps many fill with a Medigap policy. Enrollment timing around your 65th birthday matters — miss it and you face lifelong late penalties. It dominates every debate over US health spending.

plain: A private alternative to original Medicare that bundles your hospital, doctor, and often drug coverage into one plan.
snappy: Private plans paid by Medicare to deliver hospital and doctor benefits, usually with extras, in exchange for network rules.
detail: Medicare Advantage — Part C — lets a private insurer run your Medicare benefits, often adding dental, vision, and drug coverage and a capped out-of-pocket maximum that original Medicare lacks. The trade-off is networks, referrals, and prior authorization. More than half of beneficiaries now choose it. Insurers market it heavily each fall during Medicare's annual election period, and regulators scrutinise how the plans are paid.

plain: The part of Medicare that pays for hospital stays, free for most people who paid Medicare taxes while working.
snappy: The Medicare component covering inpatient hospital care, skilled nursing, hospice, and some home health, premium-free for most.
detail: Medicare Part A is the hospital half of original Medicare, covering inpatient stays, skilled nursing after a hospital admission, hospice, and limited home health. Most people pay no premium because they earned it through payroll taxes, though a deductible applies each benefit period. It pairs with Medicare Part B, and a Medigap policy can cover the leftover cost-sharing. You're usually enrolled automatically once you start drawing federal retirement benefits at 65.

plain: The part of Medicare that pays for doctor visits and outpatient care, in exchange for a monthly premium.
snappy: The Medicare component covering physician services, outpatient care, and preventive care, funded by an income-scaled premium.
detail: Medicare Part B covers what Medicare Part A doesn't: doctor visits, outpatient procedures, lab tests, durable medical equipment, and preventive care. It charges a monthly premium that rises with income, plus a deductible and 20% coinsurance with no out-of-pocket maximum — the gap a Medigap policy or a Medicare Advantage plan fills. Delaying enrollment past 65 without other coverage triggers a lifelong late penalty that catches the unwary.

plain: The part of Medicare that helps pay for prescription drugs, sold as a separate private plan.
snappy: Optional Medicare drug coverage delivered through private plans, each with its own formulary and tiered cost-sharing.
detail: Medicare Part D covers prescription drugs through private plans Medicare approves, each with its own formulary and pharmacy network. Enrollees once fell into the "doughnut hole" coverage gap, now largely closed, and recent law caps annual out-of-pocket drug costs. Skip it when first eligible without other drug coverage and a late penalty sticks permanently. Retirees re-shop Part D plans each year during Medicare's annual election period as their drugs and the formularies change.

plain: A private add-on policy that pays the deductibles and coinsurance original Medicare leaves you owing.
snappy: Standardised private insurance that covers cost-sharing gaps in original Medicare, sold in lettered plan types.
detail: Original Medicare has no out-of-pocket maximum, so a long hospital stay can pile up coinsurance. A Medigap policy fills those gaps, sold in standardised lettered plans (A through N) so the same letter means the same coverage across insurers — you shop on price and service. You can't pair Medigap with Medicare Advantage. The best time to buy is your six-month open-enrollment window at 65, when it's guaranteed issue.

plain: The bronze-silver-gold-platinum labels that sort marketplace plans by how much of your costs they cover.
snappy: ACA plan categories ranked by actuarial value: bronze pays least up front, platinum most, with premiums rising to match.
detail: Marketplace plans wear metal tiers that signal their actuarial value — the share of total costs the plan covers on average. Bronze plans have the lowest premiums but high deductibles; platinum flips it. Silver is the pivot: only silver unlocks cost-sharing reductions, so it's often the smartest buy for lower incomes. The metal label lets shoppers compare plans on the same footing before drilling into networks and formularies.

plain: The exact person or business written on the front page of the policy, with the fullest rights.
snappy: The party explicitly listed on the declarations page, holding the broadest coverage and the core duties under the policy.
detail: Being the named insured matters when a claim is contested. This party can make changes, receives notices, and enjoys coverage that may not extend to everyone in the household or company. Spouses, resident relatives, or subsidiaries may be covered automatically or only as added parties. Commercial policies often debate who should be the named insured versus an additional insured, because the distinction decides who controls the claim.

plain: The group of doctors, hospitals, and pharmacies your plan has signed up at discounted rates.
snappy: The set of providers contracted with a health plan to deliver care at negotiated rates; in-network costs you least.
detail: Your plan negotiates prices with a network of doctors and hospitals; using them triggers the lowest cost-share. Go out-of-network and you pay more — sometimes everything, plus balance billing. Whether your own doctor is in-network is the first thing to check before picking a plan or booking a procedure. A narrow network keeps premiums low by including fewer providers, a trade-off buyers often miss until they need a specialist.

plain: A 2022 law that stops you getting hit with surprise bills from out-of-network doctors you didn't choose.
snappy: A federal law barring surprise balance bills for out-of-network emergency care and certain in-network-facility services.
detail: Effective 2022, the No Surprises Act protects patients from balance billing when they couldn't reasonably pick an in-network provider — emergency care, or the out-of-network anesthesiologist at an in-network hospital. Disputes between insurer and provider go to an arbitration process instead of landing on the patient. It closed one of the most hated gaps in US health coverage and reshaped how out-of-network claims are settled.

plain: When the insurer decides not to offer you another term at the end of this one.
snappy: A decision by the insurer to end coverage at expiration rather than offer a renewal, distinct from mid-term cancellation.
detail: Nonrenewal isn't a cancellation — your current policy runs to its expiration date — but you must find a new carrier before it ends. Insurers nonrenew after too many claims, or when they pull out of a whole region, as many did from wildfire- and hurricane-exposed states. State law sets how much advance notice you're owed, giving you time to shop before going bare.

plain: A single covered event — like one accident — that the policy treats as one loss.
snappy: An event, or series of related events, that causes covered loss and counts as one incident against the policy limit.
detail: How you count occurrences decides how much coverage you have. One car crash injuring three people is usually one occurrence, capped by the per-occurrence limit; a chemical leak over months might be one occurrence or many, a distinction litigated for millions. Liability policies pair a per-occurrence limit with a larger aggregate limit so a string of separate events can't blow through the year's coverage at once.

plain: Liability cover that pays for any harm that happened while the policy was active — even if the claim comes years later.
snappy: A liability policy that responds to injury or damage taking place during its term, no matter when the claim is filed.
detail: Buy an occurrence policy for 2024 and it covers an injury caused in 2024 even if the lawsuit lands in 2030 — the trigger is when the harm happened, not when the claim arrives. That makes old policies valuable forever and removes the need for tail coverage. It's the opposite of a claims-made policy, and it's why contractors and manufacturers prize occurrence forms for long-tail risks.

plain: The yearly window when you can sign up for or change your health plan.
snappy: The annual period when people can enroll in or switch health plans without needing a qualifying life event.
detail: Outside open enrollment, you generally can't buy or change individual or marketplace coverage unless a qualifying life event opens a special enrollment period. Employers run their own open enrollment each autumn; the ACA marketplace and Medicare have their own calendars. Miss it without a qualifying event and you're locked out — or locked in — until next year. It's the deadline that drives the annual scramble to compare plans.

plain: A doctor or hospital your plan hasn't signed up — so you pay much more, or everything.
snappy: Providers without a contract with your plan; care from them costs more and may not count toward your limits.
detail: Out-of-network providers haven't agreed to your plan's rates, so the plan pays less or nothing and you can be balance-billed for the difference. HMOs and EPOs cover nothing out-of-network except emergencies; PPOs cover it at a steeper cost-share. The No Surprises Act now shields you from some out-of-network bills you couldn't avoid, like an out-of-network anesthesiologist at an in-network hospital.

plain: The yearly ceiling on what you can be forced to spend before insurance pays everything.
snappy: The annual cap on a member's combined deductible, copays, and coinsurance; beyond it the health plan pays 100%.
detail: Once your spending on covered, in-network care hits the out-of-pocket maximum, the plan pays the full cost of everything else that year. It's the real measure of financial protection a health plan offers — far more than the premium or deductible alone. The Affordable Care Act caps how high it can go. Hit it after a major surgery and the rest of the year's covered care costs you nothing.

plain: The specific cause of a loss — fire, theft, a windstorm, a crash.
snappy: A cause of loss a policy may cover or exclude, such as fire, theft, wind, water, or collision.
detail: Perils are the dangers themselves; coverage is defined by which ones the policy names. A named-perils policy lists exactly what's covered — fire, lightning, hail — and nothing else. An open-perils or all-risk form flips it, covering every cause except those excluded. Flood and earthquake are the famous ones standard homeowners policies leave out, sold instead through separate programs.

plain: The middleman that runs your plan's drug coverage and haggles prices with drugmakers.
snappy: A company that administers prescription drug benefits, builds formularies, and negotiates rebates with manufacturers.
detail: Pharmacy benefit managers sit between insurers, pharmacies, and drugmakers, deciding which drugs land on the formulary and extracting rebates in exchange for placement. The big three control most US prescriptions, and critics blame their opaque rebate model for high list prices. You never deal with one directly, but a pharmacy benefit manager shapes what you pay at the counter and which drugs your plan prefers.

plain: The written contract that spells out exactly what your insurance covers, what it won't, and what you both must do.
snappy: The legal contract between insurer and insured setting out coverage, limits, exclusions, conditions, and the premium owed.
detail: A policy is the rulebook for the whole relationship. It bundles the declarations page (your specifics), the insuring agreement (the promise to pay), exclusions (the gaps), conditions (your duties), and definitions. When an adjuster says "it's not covered," they are reading this document. Disputes over a denied claim almost always come down to a clause buried in the policy that one side read differently than the other.

plain: The most your insurer will pay for a covered loss, no matter how big the actual bill.
snappy: The maximum the insurer will pay under a coverage, per claim or in aggregate; losses above it fall back on the insured.
detail: If your liability limit is $300,000 and a court awards $500,000, you personally owe the $200,000 gap — the reason people buy umbrella insurance to stack a higher limit on top. Limits come in flavours: per-occurrence caps each event, while an aggregate limit caps the total a policy pays over its term. Choosing limits is the single biggest lever on both your premium and your protection.

plain: The window of time your coverage is active — usually six months or a year.
snappy: The span between the effective and expiration dates of a policy during which covered losses are eligible for payment.
detail: A loss has to happen inside the policy period to be covered — or, for claims-made policies, be reported inside it. Auto policies often run six months, homeowners and commercial policies a year. The renewal that arrives before expiration starts a fresh period, sometimes at a new rate. Gaps between periods are dangerous: a single uninsured day can void a mortgage or leave a crash uncovered.

plain: The person who owns the insurance policy and pays the premiums.
snappy: The party who owns the contract, pays the premium, and holds the rights to renew, cancel, or change it.
detail: Policyholder and insured often describe the same person, but not always — a company can be the policyholder of a group life plan covering its employees, who are the insureds. In a mutual insurer the policyholders are also the owners and may receive dividends. When commentators talk about "policyholder-friendly" states, they mean places where regulation tilts toward consumers in disputes over claims and rates.

plain: A hybrid health plan that uses a main doctor like an HMO but still pays a little for outside care like a PPO.
snappy: A managed-care hybrid: care is routed through a primary care physician, but out-of-network services get partial coverage.
detail: A point-of-service plan blends HMO and PPO features. You choose a primary care physician and get referrals like an HMO, but unlike one you keep some coverage when you go out-of-network — at a higher cost-share. The name refers to choosing in- or out-of-network each time you need care. Less common than HMOs and PPOs, it appears as a middle option on some employer menus.

plain: A health plan that lets you see almost any doctor without a referral, but you pay more for the freedom.
snappy: A plan that covers out-of-network care at a higher cost-share and lets members see specialists without a referral.
detail: A PPO is the flexible, pricier cousin of the HMO: you can see any doctor, skip referrals, and still get partial coverage out-of-network — though staying with preferred, in-network providers costs you far less. Higher premiums buy that freedom. Frequent travellers and people with established specialists often pay up for a PPO, while the budget-minded take an HMO.

plain: A health problem you already had before the plan started — which insurers once used to deny or overcharge you.
snappy: A medical condition predating coverage; the ACA bars insurers from denying or rating individual coverage based on it.
detail: Before the ACA, an insurer could reject an applicant with diabetes or cancer, or charge them far more. Now individual and small-group plans are guaranteed issue and community-rated, so a pre-existing condition can't keep you out or spike your premium. The protection is among the law's most popular features and the hardest for repeal efforts to touch. It's why open enrollment, not your health, governs when you can buy.

plain: The price you pay — monthly or yearly — to keep your insurance switched on.
snappy: The amount the policyholder pays the insurer for coverage, set by underwriting and actuarial pricing of the risk.
detail: Premium is the meter running on every policy. Insurers set it by estimating how likely you are to file a claim and how big it might be, then adding expenses and profit. Miss enough payments and the policy can lapse, leaving you uncovered. On an earnings call you'll hear insurers report "gross written premium" as the headline measure of how much business they wrote that year.

plain: A government subsidy that lowers the monthly cost of a marketplace health plan for low- and middle-income buyers.
snappy: An ACA subsidy that reduces marketplace premiums on a sliding scale tied to income and the local benchmark plan.
detail: The premium tax credit is what makes marketplace coverage affordable for millions: the lower your income relative to the federal poverty line, the larger the credit, applied directly to your monthly premium. It's pegged to the second-cheapest silver plan in your area. Estimate your income too low or high and you reconcile the difference at tax time, which catches many filers off guard.

plain: Checkups, screenings, and shots meant to catch problems early — covered free under most plans.
snappy: Routine screenings, vaccinations, and counselling, which ACA plans must cover with no cost-sharing when in-network.
detail: Preventive care — annual physicals, cancer screenings, immunisations, blood-pressure checks — is covered at no cost-sharing by ACA-compliant plans when you stay in-network, even before you meet the deductible. The logic is that catching disease early is cheaper than treating it late. The catch: if a screening turns diagnostic (a polyp removed during a routine colonoscopy), the visit can flip to a billable service, surprising patients who expected it free.

plain: Your main doctor — the first stop for everyday care and the one who refers you to specialists.
snappy: The general doctor who coordinates a patient's care and, in managed plans, issues referrals to specialists.
detail: A primary care physician handles checkups, common illnesses, and prevention, and in an HMO acts as the gatekeeper who must refer you before a specialist visit is covered. Building a relationship with one improves continuity of care and, plans argue, lowers costs by catching problems early. When you enroll in a managed plan you're often asked to name your primary care physician up front.

plain: The first policy to pay a loss, before any excess or umbrella coverage gets involved.
snappy: The coverage that responds first to a loss, paying from the first dollar above any deductible up to its own limit.
detail: In a tower of coverage the primary policy sits at the bottom and pays first; only when its limit is exhausted do excess and umbrella layers attach. Primary insurers also usually carry the duty to defend. When two policies could cover the same loss, "other insurance" clauses decide which is primary and which is excess — a fight that surfaces constantly in auto and commercial claims.

plain: Your plan's sign-off required before it will pay for certain drugs, tests, or procedures.
snappy: A plan's requirement that a provider get approval before a service or drug is covered, used to control cost and necessity.
detail: Prior authorization makes the doctor prove a planned MRI, surgery, or expensive drug is medically necessary before the plan agrees to pay. It's meant to curb waste but is the bane of patients and physicians who face delays and denials for needed care. Insurers and regulators are fighting over how fast decisions must come. A service delivered without required prior authorization is often denied outright.

plain: Splitting a premium or refund exactly in proportion to the time used — no penalty.
snappy: Allocation of premium or refund strictly by the share of the policy period elapsed, with no extra charge.
detail: Cancel a policy and a pro rata refund returns the unearned premium based purely on days remaining — fair and proportional. Insurers use pro rata cancellation when they end the policy, but may use short rate, which keeps a little extra, when you cancel. The phrase also describes how two insurers covering the same loss split it in proportion to their limits.

plain: The sworn statement of what you lost and what it was worth, filed to back up a claim.
snappy: A formal, often sworn, statement the insured submits documenting the loss and its value to support a claim payment.
detail: After a fire or theft the insurer asks for a proof of loss — an itemised, signed account of what was damaged and its value, with receipts or photos. It must usually be filed within a set number of days, a condition that can sink a late claim. Adjusters use it to verify the claim; a knowingly inflated proof of loss is insurance fraud.

plain: A major life change — marriage, a baby, job loss — that lets you change health coverage mid-year.
snappy: A life change that opens a special enrollment period, letting a person buy or switch coverage outside open enrollment.
detail: Marriage, divorce, the birth or adoption of a child, losing job-based coverage, or moving to a new area all count as qualifying life events. Each opens a special enrollment period so you aren't trapped by the open-enrollment calendar when your circumstances shift. Plans require proof. Knowing what qualifies is how people avoid a coverage gap after a layoff or a move.

plain: An estimated price for a policy, based on the details you give the insurer.
snappy: A non-binding estimate from the insurer of the premium for a described risk, subject to underwriting before it becomes a policy.
detail: You give an insurer your age, address, car, or health details and it returns a quote — the likely premium. Quotes are estimates: the final price can change once underwriting verifies the facts and pulls your records. Comparing quotes across carriers is the core of shopping for insurance, but matching the coverages and limits behind each number matters more than the headline price.

plain: A note from your main doctor that your plan requires before it will cover a specialist visit.
snappy: Authorization from a primary care physician for a patient to see a specialist, required by HMO and POS plans for coverage.
detail: In an HMO, seeing a dermatologist or cardiologist without a referral from your primary care physician means the plan won't pay. The referral is the gatekeeping step managed care uses to control costs and steer care. PPOs and EPOs skip it. Missing a required referral is a common reason an otherwise covered specialist claim gets denied, so patients learn to line it up first.

plain: Bringing a lapsed policy back to life by catching up and, sometimes, re-proving you qualify.
snappy: Restoring a lapsed policy to active status, usually by paying overdue premium and meeting the requirements of the insurer.
detail: After a life policy lapses, reinstatement may require back premiums plus interest and fresh evidence of insurability — a health questionnaire or exam — because your health may have changed. There's usually a time limit, often three to five years. Reinstating is generally cheaper than buying a new policy at your now-older age, so it's worth doing if you can still qualify.

plain: Continuing your policy for another term, usually with an updated price.
snappy: An offer from the insurer to continue coverage for a new policy period, often at a re-rated premium based on recent experience.
detail: Most personal policies renew automatically unless you or the insurer opts out. The renewal premium reflects a fresh look at your claims, credit-based insurance score, and market-wide rate changes — which is why a clean year can still bring an increase after a region's catastrophe losses. Reading the renewal, not just paying it, is how you catch coverage that was quietly trimmed or a deductible that crept up.

plain: Enough money to buy a brand-new equivalent of what you lost, with no deduction for age.
snappy: A settlement basis paying the full cost to repair or replace damaged property with new, without deducting depreciation.
detail: Replacement cost coverage rebuilds your roof or repays your stolen TV at today's price for a new one, unlike actual cash value which docks for age. Insurers often pay the depreciated amount first and release the rest once you actually replace the item, to keep the indemnity principle honest. It costs more in premium but spares you the depreciation gap after a major loss.

plain: The insurer unwinding a policy as if it never existed, usually because the application lied.
snappy: Cancelling a policy from inception for material misrepresentation or concealment, returning premium and denying claims.
detail: Rescission is the nuclear option: the insurer voids the contract back to day one, refunds the premiums, and treats every claim as uncovered. It's reserved for material misrepresentation or fraud on the application and is hardest to use after the contestability period closes. Health insurers were largely barred from rescinding coverage over honest mistakes by the Affordable Care Act, curbing a once-common practice after big claims.

plain: On claims-made cover, the earliest date a mistake can have happened and still be covered.
snappy: The cut-off date on a claims-made policy before which wrongful acts are not covered, even if the claim is timely.
detail: A claims-made policy with a retroactive date of 2019 won't cover a mistake made in 2018, no matter when the claim arrives. Keeping the same retroactive date when you renew or switch carriers preserves coverage for your whole career; resetting it forward creates a dangerous gap. Buyers of professional liability watch this date as closely as the limit itself.

plain: An optional extra you bolt onto a life or health policy to widen what it covers.
snappy: An add-on to a life or health policy that adds a benefit or coverage, the life-and-health cousin of an endorsement.
detail: A waiver-of-premium rider keeps your life policy in force if you become disabled; a child rider covers your kids; an accelerated death benefit rider lets a terminally ill insured tap the payout early. They let one base policy be tailored without buying a whole new contract, each adding a little premium. In property and casualty the same idea is called an endorsement.

plain: The chance that something bad and costly happens — the thing insurance exists to manage.
snappy: The uncertainty of loss that insurance prices and transfers; in industry slang, also the policy or exposure itself.
detail: Risk is the raw material of insurance. Actuaries measure it, underwriters select and price it, and reinsurers spread it. The word does double duty: "this risk" can mean a specific policy or building an underwriter is evaluating. Pooling many independent risks makes the average loss predictable even though any single one isn't — the statistical magic that lets the whole industry function.

plain: What's left of the damaged property after a claim — which the insurer can sell to recoup some of the payout.
snappy: The remaining value of property the insurer pays for in full, which it may take and sell to offset the loss.
detail: When an insurer declares a crashed car a total loss and pays its value, it takes the wreck and sells it for salvage, often to a rebuilder or parts yard. The recovery offsets the claim cost. A salvage title then warns future buyers the car was once written off. The same idea applies to fire-damaged inventory or a sunk boat the insurer paid out and now owns.

plain: An employer health plan where the company pays workers' claims itself instead of buying insurance.
snappy: An employer plan that pays employee medical claims from its own funds, usually with stop-loss cover for large losses.
detail: Large employers often self-fund: they bear the actual claims rather than paying an insurer a fixed premium, hiring an administrator to process them and buying stop-loss insurance to cap catastrophic costs. It saves money and dodges some state mandates because ERISA governs self-funded plans federally. Most big-company workers are in one without knowing it — the insurer name on the card is just the administrator.
