plain: A chunk of each loss a business pays itself before its liability policy responds — like a big deductible.
snappy: An amount the insured pays out of pocket on each claim before the liability policy attaches, common in commercial cover.
detail: Larger companies take a self-insured retention to lower premiums and keep control of small claims: they handle and pay losses up to, say, $250,000, and the insurer only steps in above that. Unlike a deductible, the insured usually manages the claim within the retention itself. It's a halfway house between buying full coverage and self-insuring entirely, and it signals an insurer that the buyer has skin in the game.

plain: A cheap, temporary medical plan that fills a coverage gap but skips many protections.
snappy: Limited-duration coverage bridging gaps between plans, exempt from ACA rules so it can deny pre-existing conditions.
detail: Short-term health insurance bridges a gap — between jobs, or before Medicare starts — at a low premium, but it's exempt from ACA rules: it can screen out pre-existing conditions, skip essential health benefits, and cap payouts. Cheap if you stay healthy, dangerous if you don't. Regulators have repeatedly tightened and loosened how long these plans can last, wary of people mistaking them for comprehensive coverage.

plain: A chance to change your health plan outside the normal window after a big life change.
snappy: A window to enroll or switch plans triggered by a qualifying life event such as marriage, birth, or loss of coverage.
detail: A special enrollment period opens when life changes — you marry, have a baby, lose job-based coverage, or move. It gives you a limited window, usually 60 days, to enroll or switch outside open enrollment. Documenting the qualifying life event is required. Losing other coverage is the most common trigger, which is why a layoff doesn't have to mean going uninsured until next year.

plain: A very expensive medication for a complex condition, often requiring special handling and the plan's pre-approval.
snappy: A high-cost drug for complex or chronic conditions, usually placed on the top formulary tier with tight management.
detail: Specialty drugs — biologics for cancer, multiple sclerosis, or rheumatoid arthritis — can cost thousands a month and sit on the highest formulary tier with coinsurance instead of a flat copay. Plans gate them behind prior authorization and step therapy and often route them through a specialty pharmacy. They're a fast-growing slice of drug spending, which is why insurers manage them so aggressively.

plain: A rule that makes you try a cheaper drug first and fail on it before the plan covers a pricier one.
snappy: A plan policy requiring patients to try lower-cost drugs before a more expensive option is covered.
detail: Under step therapy — "fail first" — your plan won't pay for the costly medication your doctor prefers until you've tried and not responded to cheaper alternatives. It saves money but can delay effective treatment, and patient groups lobby states to limit it. You'll meet it at the pharmacy counter when a prescription is rejected with a note to try the preferred drug first.

plain: Coverage that protects a self-funded employer from huge or unexpectedly high medical claims.
snappy: Insurance reimbursing a self-funded plan once claims pass a set threshold, capping the employer's medical exposure.
detail: An employer paying its own claims could be sunk by one premature baby or transplant. Stop-loss insurance caps that risk: specific stop-loss covers any single person's claims above a deductible, while aggregate stop-loss covers total claims above an expected level. It's reinsurance for self-funded plans in all but name, and it's what makes self-funding safe enough for mid-sized employers to attempt.

plain: A smaller cap inside your policy that limits payment for one specific kind of loss.
snappy: A cap below the overall policy limit applying to a particular category of loss, such as jewellery or water damage.
detail: Your homeowners policy might carry a $300,000 limit overall but a $1,500 sublimit on jewellery, so a stolen engagement ring is barely covered. Sublimits hide in the fine print and surprise people at claim time. To restore full value you schedule the item — listing it specifically for an extra premium. Commercial policies use sublimits heavily for floods, earthquakes, and cyber losses.

plain: After paying your claim, the insurer steps into your shoes to chase whoever actually caused the loss.
snappy: The right of the insurer, after paying a claim, to pursue the third party responsible and recover what it paid out.
detail: If another driver totals your car, your insurer may pay you and then subrogate — sue or bill the at-fault driver's insurer to get its money back. Successful subrogation can return your deductible to you. The principle stops the wrongdoer escaping just because you had insurance, and it keeps you from collecting twice. Health insurers subrogate too, clawing back from accident settlements they helped fund.

plain: An extension that lets you report old claims after a claims-made policy ends.
snappy: An extended reporting period on a claims-made policy that covers claims filed after expiration for prior covered acts.
detail: When a doctor retires or switches insurers, tail coverage keeps the old claims-made policy responsive to lawsuits that surface later over past treatment. Without it, every patient encounter becomes uninsured the day the policy lapses. The tail can be costly — often a multiple of the annual premium — but for long-tail professions it's the difference between a clean exit and lingering personal exposure.

plain: Insurance that pays other people for harm you caused them.
snappy: Liability coverage that pays outsiders the insured is legally responsible for injuring or whose property they damaged.
detail: When you rear-end another driver, your liability coverage is third-party — it pays the other driver, not you. The injured outsider is the third party (you and the insurer are the first two). These policies also pay to defend you against the resulting lawsuit. The insurer's duty to a third-party claimant is fair dealing, a notch below the good faith it owes its own insured.

plain: Extra liability coverage that sits on top of your home and auto policies for catastrophic claims.
snappy: A policy adding a layer of liability limit above auto, home, or business coverage, plus some broader protection.
detail: When a lawsuit blows past your auto or homeowners liability limit, an umbrella policy picks up the next million or more — cheap protection for high-net-worth families and landlords. It also fills some gaps the underlying policies exclude. Umbrellas require you to carry minimum underlying limits first, then attach above them. The name fits: one policy spreads over several others to catch the rare, ruinous claim.

plain: The part of premium you've paid for coverage that hasn't happened yet — refundable if you cancel early.
snappy: The prepaid premium covering the remaining policy period, held as a liability and refundable on cancellation.
detail: If you cancel a six-month auto policy after two months, the four months of unearned premium come back to you, minus any short-rate penalty. Insurers must hold unearned premium as a reserve — a liability on the balance sheet — because they still owe that coverage. Regulators watch the unearned premium reserve to be sure a carrier can deliver the protection it has already been paid for.

plain: The plan's process of checking whether the care you're getting is necessary and covered.
snappy: A managed-care process evaluating the medical necessity and appropriateness of services before, during, or after care.
detail: Utilization review is how a plan decides whether to pay: it judges medical necessity before treatment (prior authorization), during a hospital stay (concurrent review), or after the fact (retrospective review). Done well it curbs waste; done badly it delays needed care and frustrates doctors. It's the engine behind most coverage denials, and the appeals process exists to challenge it when a reviewer says no.

plain: The duty of both sides to deal honestly and hide nothing important when an insurance contract is made.
snappy: The doctrine that insurer and insured must each disclose all material facts honestly when forming the contract.
detail: Insurance leans on this higher duty of candour because the insured knows facts the insurer can't easily check — your health, your driving, the wiring in your warehouse. Conceal or misstate something material and the insurer may rescind the policy. The doctrine also binds the insurer to deal fairly, the seed of the bad-faith claims that punish carriers who deny coverage without reason.

plain: Paying doctors and hospitals for keeping patients healthy and getting good results, not just for doing more.
snappy: Payment models tying provider reimbursement to quality, outcomes, and cost rather than the volume of services.
detail: Value-based care rewires the incentive of fee-for-service: providers are paid partly on outcomes, patient satisfaction, and holding down total cost, often through accountable care organisations or capitation. Medicare drives the shift with programs that bonus or penalise hospitals on readmissions and quality. The promise is better care for less money; the challenge is measuring quality fairly. It's the dominant theme in how payers say they want to pay.

plain: A low-cost plan covering eye exams, glasses, and contacts.
snappy: A benefit covering routine eye exams and a periodic allowance toward glasses or contact lenses.
detail: Vision insurance is less insurance than a discount plan: for a small premium it covers an annual eye exam and gives an allowance toward frames, lenses, or contacts every year or two. Medical plans cover eye disease and injury; vision plans handle the routine wear of glasses-wearers. Bundled with dental as a voluntary benefit at work, it pays off mainly for those who buy new eyewear regularly.

plain: An employer scheme that rewards healthy habits — and can lower your premium for joining.
snappy: An employer initiative encouraging healthy behaviour, sometimes tied to premium discounts or surcharges within legal limits.
detail: Wellness programs offer biometric screenings, smoking-cessation help, or fitness incentives, often dangling a premium discount for participation. Federal rules cap how big the reward or penalty can be and bar discrimination, since a program tied too tightly to health outcomes can shade into the medical underwriting the ACA forbids. Employers pitch them as cost control; the evidence that they actually cut spending is mixed.
